K_ZBrI2LXrw.title: James O'Keefe Faces 5 Years After Minnesota Voter ID Sting
K_ZBrI2LXrw.description:
James O'Keefe and Cam Higbie entered Minneapolis polling places undercover to test Minnesota's voter identification and vouching procedures. They say they were exposing weaknesses in election security. But now Hennepin County prosecutors have charged both men with felony offenses after they allegedly used the identities of registered voters while seeking access to the ballot process—even though neither man ultimately cast a vote.

Andrew Branca examines prosecutor Mary Moriarty's announcement, the criminal complaint, and the Minnesota statutes behind the charges. The central legal question is whether falsely identifying yourself while beginning a ballot application is enough to violate the law, or whether the process must actually be completed. Andrew also explains how the identity-theft charge depends on the alleged unlawful activity and why the distinction between applying for a ballot and receiving one could determine the outcome.

But the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has now stepped in and temporarily blocked that order, raising a major question about how far federal judges can go when someone challenges a presidential administration.

I break down the emergency ruling in Red Eagle Law v. The judges did not endorse the State Department's failure to open the visa lottery, but they concluded that the law firm's claimed financial interests were insufficient to justify the relief it sought. This is an important distinction between whether the government has followed the law and who has the legal right to challenge it in court.
